value.overview: The American Herring Gull is a large, adaptable gull of North America. It breeds mainly in Canada, Alaska, the Great Lakes, and the northeastern United States, then moves south during the nonbreeding season. Adults are familiar gray-and-white gulls, while young birds remain mottled brown for several years. It uses marine shores, lakes, rivers, fields, harbors, fishing areas, and refuse sites, and is an opportunistic feeder and scavenger.
value.classification: The American Herring Gull belongs to the gull family Laridae and the order Charadriiformes. It is treated as Larus smithsonianus by several modern bird taxonomies, although some conservation assessments continue to include it within the broader Herring Gull complex.
value.identification: This is a robust, barrel-chested gull measuring about 56–66 cm long. Adults have pale gray upperparts, white underparts and head, black wingtips with small white markings, a yellow bill with a red spot, pale yellow eyes, and pinkish legs. Nonbreeding adults often show dusky streaking on the head and neck. Juveniles are mottled brown with a dark bill and tail band. Full adult plumage usually develops over four years.
value.rangeHabitat: The species breeds across much of northern North America, from Alaska and Canada south through the Great Lakes and the northeastern United States. In winter it occurs farther south through Mexico and into Central America. In Costa Rica, it is an uncommon to locally regular nonbreeding visitor rather than a breeding species, with records from coastal areas, estuaries, beaches, ports, and suitable inland wetlands or reservoirs. It may associate with other large gulls and shoreline birds.
value.migrationStatus: Migratory in much of its northern range. Many birds move south after breeding, and some reach Costa Rica during the nonbreeding season; adults may migrate shorter distances than young birds, and a few individuals can remain near breeding areas year-round.
value.breeding: American Herring Gulls usually breed colonially or in loose groups on islands, rocky shores, coastal dunes, lakeshores, and other open ground near water. Both parents defend a territory, build a ground nest of vegetation, and share incubation and chick care. A typical clutch contains two or three eggs, incubated for about a month. Chicks are fed by both parents and remain dependent for several weeks after hatching.
value.dietFeeding: The diet is highly varied and includes fish, marine invertebrates, crabs, mollusks, insects, eggs, young birds, carrion, discarded food, and refuse. The gull forages by walking along beaches and mudflats, picking items from the surface, dipping into shallow water, following fishing boats, scavenging at dumps, and feeding in fields or around human settlements. It may steal food from other birds and readily exploits temporary food sources.
value.behavior: This is a social, vocal, and competitive gull that often gathers in flocks at shorelines, harbors, reservoirs, fishing vessels, and waste sites. It spends much time resting or watching for food, but also patrols beaches and open water. Adults use loud calls and postures to defend territories and communicate. Young birds disperse widely, and immature plumages can make field identification difficult for several years.

conservation.populationTrend: Although still widespread and numerous, monitoring in parts of North America indicates a substantial long-term decline, including a pronounced decrease in the breeding population recorded by the North American Breeding Bird Survey.
conservation.threats: Important concerns include reduced availability of natural prey, contamination and pollutants, disturbance or loss of nesting habitat, entanglement and ingestion of fishing gear or plastic, and changes in waste-management practices. In some northern areas, competition or displacement by Great Black-backed Gulls may also affect breeding colonies.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect coastal and island nesting sites from disturbance, keep plastic and fishing line out of waterways, support responsible fisheries and clean waste-management practices, and avoid feeding gulls. In Costa Rica, reporting unusual or well-documented records through established bird-monitoring programs can improve knowledge of this uncommon winter visitor.
